query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated coupled degradation in multi-phase eutectic HEAs at elevated temperature is driven by cyclic mechanical loading that repeatedly disrupts the protective oxide film. The ensuing exposure of fresh, unoxidized metal accelerates both wear and corrosion, creating a positive feedback loop that exacerbates overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNiTi variant) with a microstructure capable of forming a continuous protective oxide film under high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Conduct wear-corrosion tests at 600 °C in ambient air with an electrolyte overlay, comparing static (steady sliding) conditions against cyclic (oscillatory, ~5 Hz) loading conditions while all other parameters are held constant.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (600 °C) in ambient air with a controlled electrolyte environment (e.g., dilute NaCl solution) and identical normal load for both static and cyclic loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity of the thermally induced protective oxide film on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic (oscillatory) loading, the protective oxide film is repeatedly ruptured, spalled, and then reformed. This repetitive disruption exposes fresh metallic substrate to the dual action of mechanical wear and corrosive attack. In contrast, static loading favors the development of a more uniform and adherent oxide film that better resists simultaneous wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the static baseline, the cyclic loading condition is expected to exhibit higher total degradation. This manifests as increased wear debris generation and deeper, broader wear tracks alongside higher corrosion current densities and localized corrosion attack at sites of oxide rupture.
generation.baseline: Wear-corrosion tests under static (steady sliding) mechanical loading at 600 °C with the same electrolyte exposure.
generation.boundary: The phenomenon is expected to occur under high-temperature (600 °C) conditions in an oxidizing (ambient air) environment with a consistent electrolyte (e.g., dilute NaCl), where mechanical loading is the only variable (static versus cyclic loading).
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent to which cyclic loading increases oxide rupture frequency and thereby enhances both wear and corrosion is not fully constrained; microstructural heterogeneities and slight variations in environmental conditions could modulate the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform identical high-temperature (600 °C) wear-corrosion tests with two sets of samples: one under static sliding and one under cyclic (oscillatory at ~5 Hz) loading. Use in-situ imaging (e.g., SEM or high-speed AFM) to monitor the integrity and continuity of the oxide film, along with profilometry for wear track analysis and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for corrosion assessment.
measurements: Frequency and degree of oxide film rupture (via SEM/AFM imaging)
Wear track depth and volume (using profilometry)
Corrosion current densities and impedance characteristics (via EIS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cyclic (oscillatory) loading does not produce statistically significant increases in oxide film disruption, wear track volume/depth, and corrosion rates in comparison to the static loading condition under identical environmental parameters, then the hypothesis that cyclic mechanical disruption of the oxide film drives accelerated coupled degradation would be rejected.

Such phenomenon may be evidenced by a one-time constant, a broad plateau in the range of medium frequencies (0.01–100 Hz) visible on the graph (Figure 12a), which indicates passive protection of the investigated material. Figure 12b displays the log |Z| in a function of the logarithm of the measuring frequency. The slope of log |Z| indicates the captive character of the passive film. The value of log |Z|f=0.01 Hz at low frequencies corresponds to the material’s resistance to pitting corrosion. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 was conducted as an alternative powder metallurgical production technique for high-entropy alloys (HEA). A dense microstructure of the sintered parts can be achieved. In comparison to the casting route, the fast cooling rate during atomisation suppresses the segregation of the melt and hence the precipitation of an fcc phase. The samples produced by SPS exhibit a multiphase microstructure comprising two major bcc phases. An ordered bcc phase with B2 structure and a disordered bcc phase with A2 structure are formed. In accordance with samples produced by arc-melting, a minor fcc phase is detected. Furthermore, an additional tetragonal σ-phase was detected after processing by SPS. Due to the formation of the additional phase and a microstructure with a fine phase distribution, a high microhardness of 750 ± 17 HV0.5 was determined. proposals.material_system: Multi-phase eutectic HEA similar to AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 produced by SPS
proposals.intervention: Conduct reciprocating wear-corrosion tests in simultaneously controlled atmospheres: ambient air (oxidative) versus inert (argon) environment.
proposals.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., 600 °C) under identical sliding load (constant normal force) and frequency with identical corrosive electrolyte exposure (e.g., dilute NaCl solution) at ambient pressure.
proposals.structural_mediator: Localized oxide scale formed preferentially at the eutectic phase boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: At high temperatures, the differential oxidation kinetics between the eutectic phases leads to the formation of a brittle, non-uniform oxide film at the phase boundaries. Under mechanical sliding, the oxide film cracks and spalls, exposing fresh metal that is quickly attacked by the corrosive environment. This cyclic oxide rupture and reformation synergistically accelerates both wear and corrosion.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline inert test, samples in air will show an increase in total material loss, with enhanced wear volume (due to oxidation-induced micro-cracking accelerating abrasive wear) and higher corrosion current densities (from rapid re-oxidation cycles).
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the role of oxidation-induced oxide cracking as a singular mechanism driving synergistic degradation under combined wear and corrosion, providing a controlled comparison by varying the atmospheric condition.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic HEA based on AlCoCrFeNi processed with controlled heat-treatment to modify eutectic spacing
proposals.intervention: Implement post-solidification heat treatments to vary the eutectic lamellar spacing (fine vs. coarse microstructures) followed by identical wear-corrosion tests.
proposals.conditions: Wear tests at 600 °C under identical sliding conditions and corrosive exposure (using a standardized electrolyte such as NaCl solution at room pressure), holding all other parameters constant.
proposals.structural_mediator: Interphase boundary characteristics dictated by eutectic spacing.
proposals.mechanism: Coarser eutectic spacing increases local stress concentrations and provides wider interphase regions where differential oxidation and galvanic interactions can occur. This enhances the formation and subsequent cracking of the oxide film at phase boundaries under mechanical load. In contrast, a refined microstructure reduces these vulnerabilities. The mechanism thus relates the microstructural architecture to the synergistic wear-corrosion acceleration.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the coarse-spacing baseline, the refined (fine-spaced) microstructure should display lower total degradation, with reduced wear rates and moderated corrosion responses due to diminished interphase oxidative attack.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction differentiates the effect of microstructural morphology on the coupled degradation mechanism and directly tests if the interphase boundary, influenced by eutectic spacing, is the key site for accelerated wear-corrosion interaction.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi variant) tailored for tribocorrosion studies
proposals.intervention: Perform a controlled dynamic wear experiment where the mechanical loading is modulated between static (steady) and oscillatory (cyclic) conditions while keeping environmental factors constant.
proposals.conditions: High-temperature (600 °C) wear-corrosion tests in ambient air with an electrolyte overlay, comparing static sliding versus cyclic (oscillatory) loading at a frequency of ~5 Hz.
proposals.structural_mediator: The integrity of the protective oxide film formed on the alloy surface under dynamic mechanical conditions.
proposals.mechanism: Repeated cyclic mechanical loading results in accelerated disruption and spalling of the protective oxide layer that normally forms at elevated temperature. The consequent intermittent exposure of the fresh alloy surface to the corrosive medium triggers rapid oxidative and corrosive attack. Consequently, the synergy between wear (via oxide film rupture) and corrosion (via unprotected metal exposure) is enhanced.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under oscillatory conditions, the alloy will exhibit a higher total degradation than under static loading—manifesting as increased wear debris generation and higher localized corrosion rates. In comparison to the static baseline, both wear and corrosion damage are synergistically amplified.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This research direction directly tests the hypothesis that tribochemical oxide film breakdown, driven by dynamic mechanical strain, is the singular mechanism responsible for the accelerated coupled wear-corrosion degradation.

proposals.material_system: Multi-phase eutectic HEA similar to CoCrFeMnNi with a well-defined eutectic structure
proposals.intervention: Integrate in-situ diffusion measurements using micro-probes during wear-corrosion testing, comparing conditions with and without externally imposed shear (to stimulate plastic deformation at phase boundaries).
proposals.conditions: Wear-corrosion experiments conducted at 600 °C in a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., a chloride-based electrolyte) under identical loads; one set with sustained shear (to induce plasticity at interphase boundaries) and one without such imposed shear.
proposals.structural_mediator: Interphase boundaries acting as rapid diffusion channels for corrosive species.
proposals.mechanism: Wear-induced plastic deformation at the eutectic interfaces results in microstructural disruptions that open fast diffusion pathways. These pathways rapidly channel oxygen and chloride ions along phase boundaries, accelerating local corrosion. The enhanced diffusion contributes to both increased localized corrosion and an exacerbated wear response as the structural integrity of the interphase is compromised.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to imposed shear will demonstrate deeper corrosion penetration at interphase boundaries and higher wear rates relative to the baseline (no shear) condition. The overall degradation will be quantitatively higher due to the synergy from accelerated diffusion and mechanical damage.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This candidate hypothesis singularly links wear-induced plasticity to enhanced interphase diffusion of corrosive agents. It provides a clear experimental contrast (with vs. without shear) to falsify whether rapid diffusion along damaged boundaries is responsible for the observed degradation acceleration.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly addresses the interplay between mechanical loading and environmental effects by proposing that cyclic (oscillatory) loading accelerates the rupture of the high‐temperature–formed protective oxide film. This rupture exposes fresh metal to corrosive attack, which in turn further degrades the oxide film—a synergistic feedback that clearly explains the accelerated coupled wear and corrosion. The proposed controlled comparison (static versus cyclic loading under identical high-temperature, ambient, electrolytic conditions) clearly isolates the effect of dynamic mechanical strain. While the other directions also address aspects of microstructural or diffusion‐mediated degradation, Direction D most directly targets a singular, falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis that links the integrity of the oxide film to both wear and corrosion mechanisms.
